1. Introduction

The Mikrokit is an educational computer built around the Intel 8085 microprocessor, made by Micro Design Ltd in Athens in the 1980s. It has a six-digit LED display, a 24-key keypad, two serial ports, a cassette interface and a parallel I/O connector. Its built-in program, the monitor (version 5.12), lets you examine and change memory and registers, run programs one instruction at a time, load programs over a serial line and save them on tape.

MikroKit-Emu reproduces the board on your computer. It runs the original monitor program from the kit's EPROM (only its sign-on text is changed, to "MIKROKIT MONITOR"), with the CPU running at the board's real speed (3.072 MHz, counted clock cycle by clock cycle), so programs behave as they do on the real kit, including their timing.

Emulated parts of the board:

Part Chip What you use it for
CPU 8085 runs everything
Keyboard/display controller 8279 the keypad and the 6-digit display
RAM, I/O ports, timer 8155 ports A, B, C on connector X2; single step
Serial port DB9-1 8251 the terminal
Serial port DB9-2 8085 SID/SOD program downloads
Cassette interface LM324 saving and loading programs on "tape"
Input buffer 74LS125 jumper J16 and inputs X3

Optional extras that the real kit can also have: a Tiny BASIC ROM and an HD44780 character LCD.

2. Installing and starting

Linux (ready-made program)

Unpack the archive and run the program:

tar xzf mikrokit-emu-linux-x86_64.tar.gz
./mikrokit-emu/mikrokit-emu

The folder also contains this manual's README and the examples folder with the sample programs. The ready-made program needs a recent Linux (glibc 2.44 or newer).

Windows (ready-made program)

Unzip mikrokit-emu-windows-x86_64.zip and double-click mikrokit-emu.exe in the mikrokit-emu folder. It needs Windows 10 or newer and nothing else. The folder also has the README, the manuals and the examples folder.

If the graphics driver can't run the program's normal drawing method (Vulkan or Direct3D 12), even if it crashes, the program starts again with OpenGL and remembers that OpenGL works on that PC. If that fails too, a message explains why and the report is saved in %APPDATA%\MikroKit-Emu\data\error.log. Updating the graphics driver usually helps; in a virtual machine, turn on 3D acceleration. After a driver update, start it once with mikrokit-emu.exe --renderer wgpu to use the normal method again.

Building from the source code (Linux, Windows, macOS)

Install Rust from https://rustup.rs, then in the emulator folder run:

cargo run --release

Command line

mikrokit-emu [options] [program.hex | program.asm | program.bin]
Option Meaning
--rom original start with the original monitor 5.12 (the default)
--rom basic start with the monitor + Tiny BASIC
--rom FILE use your own ROM (.bin, .hex or .asm)
--terminal start in terminal mode (jumper J16 on)
--keypad start in keypad mode (jumper J16 off)
--debug open the debug panel
--renderer wgpu / glow drawing method: Vulkan/Direct3D 12 or OpenGL (automatic by default)
program load this program into RAM at start-up
--assemble SRC [-o OUT] [--symbols] assemble a file without opening the window (see section 7)

The emulator remembers your settings (ROM, jumpers, theme, language, open windows) from one session to the next.

3. The main window

 

  1. Menu bar: File, Machine, Serial, Tape, LCD, Debug, View, Language, Help.
  2. Toolbar: pause/run the CPU, reset (the RS key), load and reload a program, choose the speed (real 3.072 MHz or Turbo), and open the tape recorder, the I/O ports window and the debug panel. The number next to the speed is the speed actually achieved.
  3. Display: the kit's six digits. The left four show an address, the right two show data.
  4. Keypad: click the keys with the mouse, or use your computer's keyboard (see section 4).
  5. Terminal: the screen of a terminal connected to serial port DB9-1.
  6. Jumpers: the board's most-used jumpers (section 13).
  7. Status bar: whether the CPU is running, the latest message, and the CPU registers (updated four times a second).

Where your typing goes. The keypad and the terminal both use your keyboard. Click the board to type on the keypad, or click the terminal to type there. The part that receives your typing has a coloured frame.

4. The keypad monitor

The keypad monitor runs when jumper J16 is off (the default). After a reset (RS), the display shows the ready message:

 

The dash on the left means the monitor is waiting for a command.

The keys

Kit key PC key Meaning
0–F 0–9, A–F hexadecimal digits
M M examine/change memory
R R examine/change registers
GO G run a program
SS S single step (one instruction at a time)
N N, Space or comma next
EX . (full stop) or Enter execute / end the command
RS F9 reset
VI F10 vector interrupt (RST 7.5, jumps to 40DFH)

Digits enter the display from the right; if you type more digits than needed, only the last ones count. A wrong key shows -Err; the dash means the monitor is still waiting for a command:

 

M: examine and change memory

Press M, type a four-digit address, then N. The display shows the address and the byte stored there:

 

  • Type two hex digits to change the byte.
  • N stores it and moves to the next address:

 

  • M (inside the command) goes back one address.
  • EX ends the command.

Memory in the ROM (0000–1FFF) can't be changed: trying shows -Err.

R: examine and change registers

Press R. The display shows register A:

 

Press N to see the next register, in this order: A, B, C, D, E, F (flags), I (interrupt mask), H, L, SPH, SPL, PCH, PCL. Type new data to change a register, and EX to finish. These are the values the monitor saved when your program last stopped (with RST 1 or a breakpoint).

GO: run a program

Press GO. The display shows the address the program will start from (the saved program counter) and the byte stored there. Type a different address if you want, then press EX to run. A program returns to the monitor with the instruction RST 1 (code CF); the display then shows the ready message again.

SS: single step

Press SS, type the start address (or keep the one shown), then press N. The CPU runs one instruction and the display shows the next address and its first byte. Each N runs one more instruction; use R to look at the registers in between. EX ends. Single step needs jumper J13 on.

Built-in programs

These ROM programs are started with GO address EX:

Address Program What the display shows
1000 write memory to tape S Ad (start address), E Ad (end address), S rC (start the recorder)
1300 read a tape into memory S rC (start the recorder)
1600 receive an Intel HEX file End when finished
1800 choose the port for 1600 POrt and the port number; press 1 or 2, then EX

5. The terminal monitor

To use the terminal monitor, switch on J16 terminal mode in the jumper bar and press RS. The monitor greets you in the terminal and shows its prompt, a full stop. Click the terminal and type commands:

 

Commands must be in capital letters; Serial → Type in capitals (on by default) does that for you. Press H for the help pages:

 

Command Meaning
X [reg] [data] … <CR> examine/change CPU registers
S addr, [data] … <CR> examine/change memory
D [start], [end] <CR> display memory
M start, end, dest <CR> move (copy) memory
G [address] <CR> run a program
T [address], … <CR> trace: run one instruction at a time
F start, end, data <CR> fill memory
E address <CR> data… <Esc> enter bytes into memory
I port, … <CR> read an input port
O port, data <CR> write an output port
P choose the serial port for L
L load an Intel HEX file
W write memory to tape
R read a tape
H help
B Tiny BASIC (only with the Tiny BASIC ROM)

Items in <> are required, items in [] are optional. <CR> is the Enter key.

Typing in the terminal

  • Enter sends CR, Backspace, Esc and Tab work as usual.
  • Ctrl+C sends ^C (it stops a BASIC program). If you have selected text, Ctrl+C copies it instead.
  • Ctrl+S / Ctrl+Q send XOFF/XON.
  • Ctrl+V pastes; pasted text is typed at a person's pace.
  • Right-click the terminal for Copy, Copy all text, Paste, Send Ctrl+C and Clear terminal.

The real monitor ignores keys pressed while it is printing. The emulator holds your typing until the monitor has finished printing, so nothing is lost.

6. Loading and running programs

Load program

Use Load program (toolbar), File → Load program, or drag a file onto the window. Supported formats:

File Contents
.hex Intel HEX: the addresses come from the file
.asm 8085 assembly source: assembled by the built-in assembler
.bin raw bytes: you are asked for the load address

After loading, the status bar shows where the program went, and the monitor's saved program counter is set to its start. So in keypad mode just press GO and EX, or type G and Enter in the terminal. (You can turn this off in Debug → Set GO address after loading a program.)

Reload loads the last file again: edit your source in any text editor, save it, press Reload, and run it again.

Programs go into RAM (2000–3FFF). Loading into the ROM area is refused.

The kit's own download

The real kit receives programs over a serial cable. You can do the same in the emulator:

  1. Start the receiving program: GO 1600 EX (keypad) or L (terminal).
  2. Send the file: Send HEX → DB9-2 (the default port of the download program) or Send HEX → DB9-1 after choosing port 1 with GO 1800 (keypad) or P (terminal).

Saving memory

File → Save memory range saves a range of addresses as an Intel HEX or binary file.

7. Writing your own programs

Write 8085 assembly in any text editor and load the .asm file directly. A minimal program:

        ORG 2000H
START:  MVI A,47H       ; A = 47H
        RST 1           ; back to the monitor
        END START

Load it, press GO and EX, then R: register A shows 47.

End your programs with RST 1 (code CF). The monitor then saves all the registers so you can look at them, and shows its prompt again.

The assembler understands labels (with or without a colon), EQU, SET, ORG, DB, DW, DS, END, strings, character constants, and expressions with + - * / MOD SHL SHR AND OR XOR NOT HIGH LOW. Numbers can be written as 2000H, 0x2000, $2000, 1010B, 17O or 17Q. Errors are reported with their line number.

To assemble without opening the window:

mikrokit-emu --assemble program.asm -o program.hex
mikrokit-emu --assemble program.asm -o program.bin --symbols

A .bin output is a full 8 KB ROM image (0000–1FFF), handy for making your own monitor ROM.

Example programs

File What it does
hello.hex puts 47H in register A and returns
count.asm counts 00–FF on the display, using the monitor's display routine
ports.asm copies the port B switches to the port A LEDs
outputs.asm sets all 8155 ports as outputs with a fixed pattern
lcd.asm writes four lines on the LCD
leds.bas Tiny BASIC: counts in binary on the port A LEDs
lcd.bas Tiny BASIC: writes to the LCD and counts 0–999

Useful addresses

Address Contents
2000–3FFF your RAM
4000–40FF the 8155's RAM; the monitor uses 40CD–40FF
40D3 / 40D6 / 40D9 / 40DC jump slots for RST 5, RST 6, RST 6.5, RST 7
40DF jump slot for VI (RST 7.5)
40E2–40EE registers saved by the monitor
40FF copy of the 8155 command register (write it when you change the CSR)

8. Monitor ROMs and Tiny BASIC

Choose the ROM in File → Monitor ROM:

 

  • Original monitor 5.12: the kit's own EPROM (the default).
  • Monitor 5.12 + Tiny BASIC: the same monitor with Palo Alto Tiny BASIC added in the ROM's free space.
  • Load from file…: your own ROM. The last file stays in the menu.

Changing the ROM resets the kit. Both ROMs are built into the emulator.

Tiny BASIC

With the Tiny BASIC ROM, J16 on (terminal mode) and RS pressed, type B at the monitor prompt:

 

  • Statements: LET (optional), PRINT, INPUT, IF (no THEN), GOTO, GOSUB/RETURN, FOR/NEXT/STEP, REM, STOP, POKE addr,value, OUT port,value, BYE.
  • Commands: RUN, LIST [line], NEW. Ctrl+C stops a program.
  • Functions: RND(n), ABS(n), SIZE (free memory), PEEK(addr), IN(port).
  • Numbers are 16-bit integers (−32768 to 32767). Variables are A–Z, and @(i) is an array. # means "not equal". Statements can be shortened with a full stop: P. = PRINT.
  • Programs live in RAM 2000–3EFF (about 7.9 KB).
  • BYE returns to the monitor; B comes back with your program still there.

To load a BASIC program from a text file, use Send HEX → DB9-1 with a .bas file: the emulator types it in line by line.

9. The tape recorder

The Mikrokit saves programs on an ordinary cassette recorder. The emulator has a virtual recorder that saves "tapes" as WAV sound files: you can even play them into a real Mikrokit, or record a real kit's tape and load it.

 

First set jumper J18 to tape (click J18 SID in the jumper bar so it says tape). The recorder window reminds you if you forget.

Writing to tape

  1. Start the write program: GO 1000 EX (keypad) or W (terminal).
  2. Give the start and end addresses.
  3. When the monitor asks you to start the recorder (S rC on the display), press Record in the recorder window, then EX (or Enter).
  4. Wait until the monitor shows its prompt again. Save WAV… keeps the tape as a file.

Reading from tape

  1. Load WAV… (or use the tape you just recorded) and press ⏮ (rewind).
  2. Start the read program: GO 1300 EX or R.
  3. Press Play, then EX (or Enter).

The MIC light shows the signal going to the recorder, the EAR light the signal coming back. Click the waveform to move the tape head.

10. The I/O ports

The I/O ports window (toolbar or View menu) shows the parallel port connector X2 and the input buffer:

 

  • Ports A, B and C of the 8155 (I/O addresses 41H, 42H, 43H). A port set as an output is shown as red LEDs; a port set as an input is shown as blue switches you can click. The direction follows the 8155's command register (port 40H).
  • Port 3EH: the three inputs on connector X3 (bits D0–D2).
  • Port 0FH: jumper J16 on bit D0 (0 = terminal monitor).
  • The 8155 timer, which the monitor uses for single stepping.

Try outputs.asm (all three ports as outputs) and ports.asm (switches on port B light the LEDs on port A).

11. The LCD

You can connect a 16x2 or 20x4 character LCD (HD44780 compatible) to the 8155's port B, in 4-bit mode. Choose it in the LCD menu:

 

 

Wiring

8155 pin Connector X2 LCD
PB2 pin 15 RS
PB3 pin 16 E
PB4 pin 13 D4
PB5 pin 14 D5
PB6 pin 11 D6
PB7 pin 12 D7
— ground D0–D3, R/W
— pins 2, 4 (+5V) / 1, 3 (ground) power

Programming it

  • Set port B as an output: write 02H to the 8155 command register (port 40H), and keep a copy at 40FFH.
  • Send each byte as two halves (the high four bits first) on PB4–PB7, with RS on PB2 (0 = command, 1 = character), and pulse E (PB3) high then low for each half.
  • Start-up: send 3, 3, 3, then 2 (as single halves) to switch the LCD to 4-bit mode, then the commands 28H (2 lines), 0CH (display on), 01H (clear) and 06H (move right).
  • Because R/W is tied to ground, a program can't ask the LCD whether it is ready; it has to wait: about 40 µs after each byte and 1.6 ms after Clear (01H) or Home (02H). If your program is too fast, the LCD window shows a warning: a real LCD might lose those bytes.

examples/lcd.asm shows all of this; examples/lcd.bas does the same in Tiny BASIC (BASIC is slow enough to need no delays).

The menu also offers a blue backlight and Power cycle the LCD. Before a program sets it up, a real LCD shows a row of dark blocks; the emulated one does the same.

 

The LCD shows all the standard characters (codes 20H–7FH), the eight characters you can design yourself (codes 00H–07H), and a few symbols from the upper half (°, µ, Ω, π, the solid block). The Japanese katakana characters are shown blank.

12. The debug panel

Open it with Debug on the toolbar:

 

  • CPU: all registers, the flags, and the interrupt state.
  • Pause / Run, Step, Step ×100: stop the CPU and run one or a hundred instructions.
  • Disassembly: the next instructions; ▶ marks the current one, ● a breakpoint.
  • Breakpoints: type an address and press Add. The CPU pauses when it reaches it.
  • Memory: 64 bytes from any address (quick buttons for RAM, the 8155 and ROM).
  • Monitor's saved user registers: what the R command will show.
  • The state of the 8155 ports and timer.

Turbo speed (toolbar) runs the CPU as fast as your computer can, which is handy for long BASIC programs. Timing-dependent things (the tape, the serial port on DB9-2) still work, because they follow the emulated clock.

13. Jumpers

The jumper bar at the bottom changes the board's jumpers; the Machine menu has the same settings.

Jumper Setting Effect
J16 on / off terminal monitor / keypad monitor (press RS after changing it)
J13 on the 8155 timer drives TRAP (needed for SS and T)
J18 DB9-2 / tape SID and SOD go to serial port DB9-2 or to the tape interface
J17 position 1–11 baud rate of DB9-1: 9600 (position 1), 4800, 2400, 1200, 600, 300 …
J14 on the 8155 RAM is enabled at 4000H

The other jumpers on the board (J1–J12) set interrupt pull-downs and the memory chip types. The emulator is fixed at the standard setting: 2764 EPROM and 6264 RAM.

14. Appearance and language

  • View → Follow the system / Dark / Light chooses the colours. In the light theme the terminal shows dark text on a light background:

 

  • Language → English / Ελληνικά switches the whole program between English and Greek. Text printed by the kit itself (the monitor, BASIC) stays as the ROM has it.
  • View also opens the tape recorder, the I/O ports window and the debug panel.

16. Troubleshooting

Problem Solution
Nothing happens when I type Click the part you want to type into (the board or the terminal); it gets a coloured frame.
The terminal stays empty Turn on J16 terminal mode and press RS.
The monitor ignores my commands Commands must be in capitals; keep Serial → Type in capitals on.
Single step does nothing J13 must be on.
The tape doesn't record or read J18 must be set to tape. Press Record/Play before the last EX. Rewind before reading.
A download doesn't arrive Send to the port the download program is listening on (DB9-2 by default; choose with GO 1800 or P).
My program doesn't return End it with RST 1. Press RS to get the monitor back.
The LCD shows dark blocks The program hasn't set it up yet, or port B isn't an output.
The LCD window warns about busy writes Add delays: 40 µs per byte, 1.6 ms after Clear/Home.

MikroKit-Emu. The Mikrokit was designed by Micro Design Ltd. Tiny BASIC is Palo Alto Tiny BASIC by Li-Chen Wang and Roger Rauskolb (1976).
